titleEn: Chainsaw Laceration to the Thigh - Tourniquet Plus Junctional Wound Packing

patient.name: Glen Hartley
patient.affectEn: alert but pale, sweating and shivering; frightened by the amount of blood; sitting in the mud against a stack of firewood rounds gripping his left thigh
patient.speechEn: full sentences, voice shaky from cold and fear; cooperative and follows instructions; answers what is asked and keeps saying the saw 'just jumped back at me'

scene.settingEn: Private woodlot off Sylvester Road, Mission, mid-afternoon. Steady cold rain, 6 degrees C. A gravel road ends at an open gate; from the gate about 40 metres of wet, uneven, slippery ground lead down to the work site. The chainsaw lies switched off on the ground three metres from the patient with the chain brake engaged. The patient sits in the mud against a stack of rounds. One patient. Mission Fire first responders are a few minutes behind you. Abbotsford Regional Hospital is 26 minutes by road; air ambulance is unavailable because of low cloud.
hazardsEn: chainsaw - switched off on the ground three metres away with the chain brake engaged; confirm before approaching
arterial blood - splash exposure; an estimated 800 to 1000 mL already in the mud
wet, uneven, slippery slope - about 40 metres between the gate and the patient
steady cold rain, 6 degrees C - exposure for the patient and the crew

bystanders.knowsEn: His father was cutting firewood when the saw kicked back into his left thigh; it happened a few minutes before he made the call. There was blood everywhere, so he cinched his leather belt around his father's leg and then called 911 from his phone. He opened the gate and waved you down. He does not know anything about his father's medical history beyond 'he takes a blood pressure pill'. He will carry, hold a light, fetch blankets or meet the fire crew at the gate - but only if told exactly what to do.

bystanders.who: Mission Fire first responders (arrive a few minutes after you)
bystanders.knowsEn: Nothing about the patient. They bring extra hands, lighting, blankets and a scoop or basket stretcher for the carry-out, and act only on your direction.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: scoop or basket stretcher (brought by the fire crew)
cot (left at the gate - it cannot be wheeled down the slope)
PCP: IV start kit and tubing

dispatchEn: 1420 hrs. Code 3 to a private woodlot off Sylvester Road, Mission. A 47-year-old male was bucking firewood when the chainsaw kicked back into his left thigh. The caller is his son. Steady cold rain, 6 degrees C. Mission Fire first responders are 6 minutes behind you. Abbotsford Regional Hospital is 26 minutes by road; air ambulance is unavailable because of low cloud.
dispatchUpdateEn: En-route update: the son says there is 'blood everywhere' and that he has cinched a leather belt around his father's leg. Access is a gravel road with a gate at the top and about 40 metres of uneven ground down to the work site.
arrivalEn: The gate at the top of the gravel road is open and the son waves you down the slope. About 40 metres of wet, uneven, slippery ground lead down to the work site. Steady cold rain, 6 degrees C. The chainsaw is switched off on the ground three metres from the patient with the chain brake engaged. One patient. No other hazards. Mission Fire has not arrived yet.
firstLookEn: A 47-year-old man sitting in the mud against a stack of firewood rounds, awake and watching you; pale, sweating and shivering, gripping his left thigh. His left pant leg is shredded and soaked. A leather belt is cinched around the thigh above the wound, but bright red blood is still pumping from the mid-front of the left thigh and running into the mud - an estimated 800 to 1000 mL is already on the ground.

primary.locEn: Alert. Oriented to person, place, time and event; frightened but answers appropriately. (AVPU = A.)
primary.airwayEn: Open and clear. Speaking in full sentences, no blood or debris in the mouth, no stridor.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 24, regular, adequate depth, equal chest rise, not laboured, no accessory muscle use. If SpO2 is checked now: 92% on room air; 97% once on 15 L by non-rebreather.
primary.circulationEn: Right radial pulse 128, weak and thready, regular. Major external bleeding from the left thigh (see the RBS). Together with the pale, cool, clammy skin this is hypovolemic shock.
primary.rbsEn: LEFT THIGH: a deep chainsaw laceration across the mid-front of the left thigh with bright red blood pumping from it. The son's leather belt above the wound is loose and controls nothing. If the candidate applies direct pressure through dressings: it SLOWS the bleeding but does NOT stop it - blood keeps welling through. Do not suggest a tourniquet. If the candidate removes the belt and applies the commercial windlass tourniquet high and tight on the left thigh, proximal to the wound, over skin, tightened until the bleeding stops and the distal pulse is gone: the thigh wound stops bleeding. If the candidate only tightens or re-ties the belt, or leaves the belt as the tourniquet, the bleeding does not stop (report belt-relied-on). If the time of application is never stated, do not remind them (report tourniquet-time-not-noted). ONCE THE TOURNIQUET IS ON (or as soon as the candidate exposes and looks at the left groin): a second deep gash in the left groin crease keeps bleeding steadily. It is junctional - a tourniquet cannot be placed above it. If the candidate packs it firmly with gauze down to the bleeding source, holds sustained direct pressure and then applies a pressure dressing over the packing: the groin bleeding is controlled and the dressing stays dry. A second tourniquet does not control it (report groin-tourniquet-attempt). Rest of the RBS: no other injuries - head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, back, right leg and both arms are unremarkable. No fall, no head strike, no loss of consciousness: spinal precautions are NOT indicated. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: pale, cool, clammy.

history.ccEn: My leg. The saw kicked back into my thigh and it won't stop bleeding.

opqrst.oEn: All at once. I was limbing a wet alder at full throttle, the tip caught and the saw kicked back into my thigh. It just jumped back at me. That was about five minutes before my son called 911 for me.
opqrst.qEn: It just hurts, bad, right where the saw went in.
opqrst.rEn: It's in my left thigh and up in my groin. Nowhere else.
opqrst.sEn: Before the tourniquet is on: "Nine out of ten." After the tourniquet is on: "About a seven now."
opqrst.tEn: Since the saw hit me - about five minutes before the call. It hasn't let up.

history.painScoreEn: 9 out of 10 before the tourniquet; 7 out of 10 once the tourniquet is on

sample.sEn: My leg is cut open and I've lost a lot of blood. I'm freezing and shaking, my heart is pounding, and I felt faint when I tried to stand up.
sample.aEn: No allergies that I know of.
sample.mEn: Ramipril, for my blood pressure. That's all I take.
sample.pEn: High blood pressure. I had an arthroscopy on my left knee in 2018. Nothing else - no heart problems, no bleeding problems. (Only if asked about tetanus: "My last tetanus shot was about ten years ago, I think.")
sample.lEn: A sandwich and a coffee at 1300.
sample.eEn: I was limbing a wet alder at full throttle and the tip caught - the saw kicked back into my thigh. I wasn't wearing chaps. I didn't fall, I didn't hit my head, and I never blacked out. Only the leg got cut.

fe.generalEn: I felt faint when I stood up after it happened. Before today I was well - no recent illness.
fe.cnsEn: No, I never blacked out. No headache.
fe.respiratoryEn: My breathing's fine. No cough, no chest tightness.
fe.cardiovascularEn: My heart is pounding. No chest pain.
fe.giGuEn: I felt sick once, but I haven't thrown up. No belly pain, no problems with my bowels or bladder.
fe.integumentaryEn: Just the cuts on my thigh and in my groin. Nothing else.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: I can't put any weight on my left leg. Nothing else hurts - my neck, back, arms and other leg are fine.
fe.endocrineEn: Nothing. No diabetes, no thyroid problems.
fe.eentEn: Nothing. My eyes, ears, nose and throat are fine.

findings.headNeckEn: Normal. No injury above the clavicles; no tenderness or deformity of the scalp, face or neck. Trachea midline, no JVD.
findings.chestLungsEn: Chest clear with equal air entry at all 6 sites. No tenderness, no deformity, equal rise and fall.
findings.abdomenEn: Soft and non-tender in all four quadrants. No distension, no bruising.
findings.backEn: Checked during the transfer: no injury, no tenderness, no deformity.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: LEFT: windlass tourniquet on the proximal left thigh (with the time written on it if the candidate marked it); thigh wound bandaged with no further bleeding; packed and dressed left groin wound, dressing staying dry. No pulse in the left foot and the left foot is cool - expected below a tourniquet. RIGHT leg: entirely normal, strong pedal pulse, normal movement and sensation.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: Normal. No injuries; radial pulses present in both arms; normal movement, sensation and grip. Either arm can take the BP cuff and the SpO2 probe.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: baseline in the ambulance; tourniquet on at 1430, groin packed at 1433, set taken at 1436
en route (1444 in the model timeline), after warming and high-flow oxygen; bleeding remains controlled

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: Blood is still pumping from the left thigh into the mud. The patient is visibly paler, his radial pulse is faster and harder to feel, and he says: "I feel like I'm going to pass out."
The thigh wound has stopped bleeding, but blood is still welling steadily from the gash in the left groin crease and pooling under his hip. He is getting paler.
As soon as the tourniquet loosens, bright red blood pumps from the thigh wound again and the patient becomes paler and more frightened.
As the packing comes out, blood wells up from the groin wound again and fills it quickly. The patient groans and looks paler.
He is shivering hard now, teeth chattering, still lying on the cold wet ground in his soaked clothes.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge the call and plan the sequence out loud: tourniquet, wound packing, high-flow oxygen, warmth, early transport
triggers: this will be a load and go

expected.actionEn: Request fire first responders for the carry-out and extra hands; confirm gate access and a carry route; consider a PCP/ALS intercept given the 26-minute road time
Anticipate blood exposure, a running saw, wet uneven ground and cold rain; prepare PPE including eye protection and high-visibility clothing
Verbalize hazards (saw shut down, blood, slippery slope, cold rain), environment, MOI (chainsaw kickback) and number of patients
Don gloves and eye protection before touching the patient (arterial splash risk)
First look from the approach: pale, sweating, anxious adult male, awake, pumping bright red blood from the mid-anterior left thigh
Direct the son and the arriving fire crew: bring the cot to the gate, prepare blankets, plan the 40-metre carry

can you meet the fire crew

expected.actionEn: Remove the ineffective belt and apply a commercial windlass tourniquet high and tight proximal to the thigh wound; tighten until bleeding stops; NOTE THE TIME; never release
Pack the junctional groin wound with gauze and hold sustained direct pressure, then apply a pressure dressing - a tourniquet cannot be used there (never pack neck, chest or abdomen)

expected.actionEn: Execute hypovolemia management: supine, high-flow oxygen, warmth, rapid transport
Verbalize that Entonox is withheld because shock is a listed caution, and document the rationale
Active rewarming: remove wet clothing, dry the patient, blankets, ambulance heat up - cold worsens bleeding
Reassess ABCs plus the tourniquet and both dressings after each move
Second complete set of vitals within 5-6 minutes and interpret the trend out loud
Never loosen or release the tourniquet and never remove the packing en route
Keep monitoring temperature and continue rewarming

Complete verbal hand-off including tourniquet time, packing site, blood loss, warming and tetanus status
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes with both hemorrhage-control times documented

specialEvents.descriptionEn: the commercial windlass tourniquet is actually applied to the left thigh and tightened (the act itself, not a plan to apply one)
the left groin wound is actually packed with gauze (the act itself, not a plan to pack it)

candidate actually starts protecting the patient from the cold: gets him off the wet ground onto insulation or a blanket, removes or cuts off the wet clothing, dries him, covers him with blankets, or turns the ambulance heat up

candidate uses the son's leather belt as the tourniquet - tightens or re-ties it, or leaves it as the only constriction on the thigh - instead of removing it and applying the commercial windlass tourniquet

after direct pressure has failed on the thigh, or after the groin bleed has been found, the candidate keeps relying on direct pressure alone or moves on to vitals, history, oxygen, the physical exam, packaging or the carry-out while that bleed is still uncontrolled (a quick airway and breathing check while the partner holds pressure is NOT this event)
tourniquet placed distal to the thigh wound, over the belt or over thick wet clothing instead of over skin, not tightened until the bleeding stops, or not secured (windlass left loose)
candidate loosens, releases, converts or removes the tourniquet at any time after it is applied (including 'to check whether it is still bleeding')
tourniquet applied but the candidate never states, writes or asks for the time of application

candidate actually tries to control the junctional groin bleed with a second tourniquet instead of packing it, or packs a wound of the neck, chest or abdomen (saying that a tourniquet cannot be used in the groin is NOT this event)
the groin wound is packed loosely or only on the surface, sustained direct pressure is not held on the packing, or no pressure dressing is applied over the packing
candidate pulls out or removes the original groin packing (for example to look at the wound) instead of adding more packing and pressure on top of it

candidate applies a hard collar, keeps manual c-spine stabilization beyond the brief screening questions, or immobilizes this patient on a spinal device although there was no fall, no head strike and no spinal mechanism
candidate lets or asks the patient to stand, bear weight, walk or hop at any point, including up the slope to the gate
candidate keeps the patient on scene or in the parked ambulance to wait for the PCP/ALS intercept instead of departing and meeting the intercept en route
PCP runs the saline bolus past 500 mL or onto the next bag without reassessing the patient (BP / vitals / ABCs) in between

drugs.doseEn: self-administered by inhalation - WITHHELD in this scenario: shock is a listed caution (record drug:entonox only if it is actually given)
drugs.contraindicationsEn: inability to comply; inability to ventilate an enclosed treatment area; decompression sickness; altered level of consciousness; pneumothorax; air embolism; inhalation injury; nitroglycerin in the last 5 minutes
drugs.cautionsEn: shock; abdominal distention; depressant drugs; COPD; facial injuries

drugs.doseEn: 3 mL self-administered via inhaler per guideline - NOT indicated here: the indication is pain in a conscious, hemodynamically stable patient and this patient is in shock (record only if actually given)
500-1000 mg PO per guideline - NOT part of this call: hypovolemia is a listed caution and a shocked patient going to the operating room gets nothing by mouth (record only if actually given)
300-400 mg PO per guideline - NOT part of this call: a shocked patient going to the operating room gets nothing by mouth (record only if actually given)
2 g (2000 mg) IV push over 1 minute - single dose
drugs.indicationsEn: major trauma after initiating the Hypovolemia protocol; shock from blood loss; injury at about 1415 is well inside the 3-hour window
drugs.contraindicationsEn: known hypersensitivity or allergy to TXA; more than 3 hours after injury; patient under 12 years; isolated TBI
drugs.cautionsEn: further hypotension if administered too quickly

drugs.doseEn: 20 mL/kg IV bolus to a maximum of 2 L, reassessing after every 500 mL; target systolic around 90

examinerPrompts.missedInjuryEn: You have dealt with the thigh wound - what did the rest of your rapid body survey find? Is there any other bleeding?

trackNotes.emrEn: EMR scope covers everything this patient needs before hospital: commercial windlass tourniquet, junctional wound packing, pressure dressings, high-flow oxygen, supine positioning, aggressive rewarming and a 15-minute package. IV access, a fluid bolus and TXA are PCP-only and are not acceptable answers at EMR level. Entonox is within EMR scope but is withheld because shock is a listed caution - say so out loud; methoxyflurane needs a hemodynamically stable patient and the oral analgesics are not for a shocked patient going to surgery. Request a PCP/ALS intercept for the 26-minute road time but never delay departure to wait for it.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds vascular access en route, a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus to a maximum of 2 L reassessed every 500 mL targeting a systolic around 90, and TXA 2 g IV over 1 minute (well inside the 3-hour window, shock from blood loss), plus the Functional Enquiry en route. The hemorrhage control itself does not change - the tourniquet and the packing are what save this leg and this life.

sourcePages: Scenario etr-07 (data/practical/emr-trauma-2.json): dispatch, scene, primary, transport, history, vitals sets 1-2, FE, exam, interventions, ongoing, handoff, critical pitfalls, EMR/PCP variants. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (hemorrhage requiring tourniquet application or wound packing; cool pale clammy skin secondary to suspected shock); p.19 Wound Care (direct pressure first; tourniquet proximal to the wound if pressure fails; junctional hemorrhage not amenable to a tourniquet - consider wound packing; do not pack wounds of the neck, chest or abdomen; tourniquet: note the time and do not release once applied; bandage once controlled); p.29 Hypothermia (remove wet and cold clothing, cover with blankets, take temperature, preheat the ambulance); p.54 Hypovolemia (control external hemorrhage, supine, keep warm, oxygen to SpO2 94% or above; PCP: vascular access, 20 mL/kg bolus to a maximum of 2 L reassessing every 500 mL, consider TXA in shock secondary to blood loss); p.58-59 Acetaminophen (500-1000 mg PO; caution: hypovolemia); p.65 Entonox (indication: isolated extremity injuries; caution: shock); p.68 Ibuprofen (300-400 mg PO); p.71 Methoxyflurane (indication: pain in conscious, hemodynamically stable patients); p.78 Tranexamic Acid (2 g IV push over 1 minute; contraindicated more than 3 hours after injury). EMALB Practical Examination Grading Criteria timing rules (priority patient ready to load in 15 minutes; vitals interval moderate 7-8 / major over 9 minutes).
